title: Hydrocele
subject: Surgery
summary: A hydrocele is a fluid collection between the tunica vaginalis layers, usually painless and non‑acute. In low‑resource settings, filariasis and secondary causes are common. Diagnosis is clinical, with ultrasound if available.

sections.p: Hydrocele is serous fluid between the visceral and parietal tunica vaginalis. It is the most common cause of a painless scrotal swelling in adults.

t.b: Is the swelling reducible? A non‑communicating hydrocele does not reduce; a communicating one changes with posture.
Shows anechoic fluid with thin septa; distinguishes hydrocele from hernia or tumor.
WBC count, eosinophils, filarial antigen or microfilariae on night‑time smear.

sections.p: Hydrocele is usually classified by size and effect on testis: small, moderate, large. Large hydroceles (>5 cm) may cause discomfort or impair spermatogenesis.
In East Africa, filariasis is the leading acquired cause. Others include infection, trauma, surgery, radiotherapy, and idiopathic primary hydrocele.
b: Secondary to epididymo‑orchitis, trauma, surgery, radiotherapy

sections.p: A smooth, non‑tender, fluctuant scrotal mass that may increase with standing and decrease when lying supine. No systemic signs unless secondary infection.
b: Reduces with lying down if communicating

sections.p: Clinical exam is key; imaging and labs are adjuncts when available.

t.b: Confirms fluid collection, rules out hernia or tumor; shows septations.
Positive in active infection; guides anti‑filarial therapy.
Eosinophilia suggests filariasis; leukocytosis indicates infection.

sections.p: Urgent signs include sudden pain, swelling, fever, or signs of infection. Complications can be testicular atrophy, infertility, or, rarely, malignant transformation.
b: Acute pain or fever – consider infection or torsion
Large hydrocele – risk of testicular atrophy

sections.p: Treat underlying cause first. Symptomatic hydroceles are managed with aspiration or surgery; filarial hydroceles require anti‑filarial drugs.

t.b: Used for small, symptomatic hydroceles; repeat if fluid re‑accumulates.
Less invasive than surgery; effective for small to moderate hydroceles.
Preferred for large, persistent, or complicated hydroceles; involves stripping the sac and preserving the testis.

sections.p: Monitor for recurrence, testicular function, and signs of filariasis. Prevention focuses on vector control and early treatment of filarial infection.
b: Annual filariasis screening in endemic areas

sections.p: Inguinal hernia, epididymitis, testicular tumor, varicocele.
b: Hernia – reducible, may have cough impulse

sections.p: Ultrasound may miss a small communicating hydrocele; filarial antigen can be negative early in infection.
b: Small fluid pockets may be overlooked

faq.a: The fluid itself is benign; however, a large hydrocele can mask a testicular tumour, so any change in size or pain warrants evaluation.

faq.q: Is aspiration safe in all cases?
faq.a: It is safe for small, uncomplicated hydroceles but has a high recurrence rate; surgery is preferred for large or recurrent cases.

faq.q: What if ultrasound is not available?
faq.a: Rely on clinical exam: a non‑tender, fluctuant, non‑reducible swelling that changes with posture suggests hydrocele; consider empirical treatment if filariasis is suspected.

exam: 1. A 35‑year‑old man presents with a painless, enlarging scrotal swelling that reduces when he lies down. What is the most likely diagnosis and first step in management? — Hydrocele; perform scrotal ultrasound if available, otherwise consider aspiration or surgical referral.
2. In a filariasis endemic area, a patient has a chylous scrotal fluid collection. What drug should you start and why? — Diethylcarbamazine; it kills microfilariae and reduces fluid production.
3. A 28‑year‑old man has a large, non‑reducible scrotal mass. What sign distinguishes it from an inguinal hernia? — Absence of cough impulse and lack of reducibility.

4. A patient with a hydrocele develops sudden pain and fever. What is the urgent differential and immediate action? — Infection or testicular torsion; urgent scrotal exploration or incision and drainage.
5. Why is sclerotherapy with doxycycline preferred over surgery in some settings? — It is less invasive, can be done bedside, and avoids anesthesia risks in low‑resource hospitals.
6. A hydrocele recurs after aspiration. What is the next best step? — Surgical hydrocelectomy to remove the sac and prevent recurrence.
7. How can you differentiate a hydrocele from a varicocele on exam? — Hydrocele is fluctuant and non‑tender; varicocele is a cord‑like, often tender, “bag‑of‑peanuts” swelling.
8. What laboratory finding would support filarial etiology in a hydrocele? — Eosinophilia or positive filarial antigen test.
